::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, October 2026.** All figures are my own, drawn with the code in [figs.py](figs.py). Figures 3 and 5 use numbers from the studies cited in their captions; the others are schematics.
:::

**In short.** AI is getting very good at solving problems, and it will keep getting faster. If we measure ourselves by the pace at which we find answers, we have already lost, and it does not matter. Machines taking work from us has happened before, and each time people who kept learning climbed to harder and more interesting things. What remains ours is setting the problems, which asks for creativity, imagination and judgement, and, underneath, caring about them. A machine does not care whether a question matters. We do. Even if the deepest questions stay out of reach for us and for any machine, the motivation to pursue them, the meaning we find on the way and the joy of the climb may be what matters most. The risk is that we hand over the effort that builds these things, and children most of all.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Key takeaways

- Solving is being automated fast. Even the strongest discovery systems still need a person to say what counts as a good answer [@novikov2025alphaevolve].
- Losing work can lift us. After superhuman Go programs appeared, professional players made better and more novel moves [@shin2023].
- The same AI tool widens the gap between people. Entrepreneurs who were already strong gained over 15%; weaker ones lost about 10%. What differed was which advice they chose to follow [@otis2026].
- Effort is how skill and motivation grow. Students who practised with a plain chatbot did 17% worse once it was taken away [@bastani2025]; workers who moved from AI-assisted to solo work felt less motivated and more bored [@wu2025].
- The skills that stay ours are creativity, imagination and epistemic literacy: telling information from knowledge.
- Philosophers saw this long ago. Einstein put the formulation of a problem above its solution, Nietzsche put the *why* before the *how*, and Spinoza defined joy as our own power to act growing.
- A machine works on whatever it is given. Choosing what is worth our life, and enjoying the pursuit, is not a task to automate.
:::

## 1. The wrong race

In July 2025, an AI system reached gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad [@deepmind2025imo]. A few weeks earlier, a coding agent had found a way to multiply two 4×4 complex matrices with 48 multiplications, the first improvement in 56 years on this case [@novikov2025alphaevolve]. Since then, the list of results once reserved for specialists and now claimed by machines has kept growing.

The usual reaction is a race: how long before the machine is faster than me at *my* work? I think this is the wrong race. Speed is the one thing a machine will always win. A better question is what we are for, once speed is no longer our job.

Look at how such systems actually work. To run AlphaEvolve, a person writes down the problem and a program that scores any proposed answer. The machine then searches, far faster than we could. Without that scoring function there is nothing to search for. And behind the scoring function there is something even more human: a reason to care about this problem rather than another.

Figure 1 is how I picture it. In the middle is *how*: solving. Machines take more of it every year. Around it is *which*: which problem, and what counts as a good answer. Around that is *why*: why it matters to us at all. The outer rings are not slower versions of the middle one. They are a different kind of thing.

Nietzsche wrote that whoever has a *why* to live can bear almost any *how* [@nietzsche1889]. He was writing about suffering, not software, but the order he gives holds here too: the why comes first, and it gives the how its worth. Machines are taking the how. The why was never theirs.

![**Figure 1.** Three layers of a problem. Machines take over the *how*. The *which* asks for creativity and judgement. The *why*, caring whether it matters, belongs to us. Schematic, my own.](figures/fig01.svg){fig-alt="Three concentric circles. The core, dark blue, is HOW: solve; machines do more of it, faster every year. The middle ring, amber, is WHICH: noticing, framing, choosing, checking; creativity, imagination and judgement. The outer ring, green, is WHY: care, motivation, meaning, the reason to start and the joy of the climb; no machine needs it."}

## 2. Losing work, gaining height

Machines have taken work from us before. Calculators took arithmetic, spell checkers took spelling, search engines took a large part of remembering. Each time, people feared we would become less capable. Each time, those who kept learning used the freed time to climb.

Games give us the cleanest evidence, because the quality of a move can be measured. Researchers scored more than 1.6 million moves from professional chess games played between 1890 and 2014 against a chess engine's best move. Play improved over the decades, and press coverage of the study linked a sharp rise in the 1990s to players gaining access to strong computer opponents [@strittmatter2020]. In Go, a study of 5.8 million moves by professional players from 1950 to 2021 found that after superhuman AI appeared in 2016, human moves became better, and more novel: players started trying moves no one had played before, and those new moves were good [@shin2023]. The machines did not end the game. They showed people that the space was bigger than they thought.

![**Figure 2.** Losing work, gaining height. As machines take over a kind of work, what people choose to learn and attempt can rise above it. The upper line only rises if we keep climbing. Schematic, my own; the two notes summarise @strittmatter2020 and @shin2023.](figures/fig02.svg){fig-alt="A step chart over time. A lower blue staircase, work handed to machines, rises from arithmetic in 1950 to calculation in 1975, chess moves in 1997, Go moves in 2016, and code, essays and proofs in 2023. A dashed amber staircase above it, what people choose to learn and attempt, rises as well. Notes: after strong chess engines the quality of human play rose; after AlphaGo professionals played better and more novel moves."}

This is the hopeful half of my argument. Losing much of our work may let us learn more advanced things than we ever had time for. But the upper line in Figure 2 does not rise by itself. It rises only for people who keep climbing, and climbing is effort.

## 3. Same tool, different people

Will AI make everyone equally capable? The evidence says: it depends on who sets the problem.

When the problem is set by someone else and good answers are known, AI tends to close gaps. In a call centre with over 5,000 agents, an AI assistant raised productivity by 15% on average, mostly for the least experienced; the best agents gained little [@brynjolfsson2025].

When people must set the problem themselves, the picture changes (Figure 3). In a field experiment with 758 consultants, those using AI on tasks it handles well completed 12.2% more tasks and worked 25.1% faster. On a task chosen to lie just beyond what it could do, they were 19 percentage points *less* likely to reach the right answer than colleagues without AI [@dellacqua2026]. The tool did not say where its competence ended. Knowing that was the person's job. In Kenya, 640 small business owners were given an AI mentor. On average nothing changed. But owners who were already doing well improved by over 15%, while those who were struggling did about 10% worse. Both groups asked similar questions and got similar advice. What differed was *which advice they chose to act on* [@otis2026].

![**Figure 3.** Same tool, different people. Consultants with AI on tasks inside and just beyond what AI does well [@dellacqua2026], and entrepreneurs with an AI mentor by performance before the study [@otis2026]. Percent changes, except the consultants' correct answers, in percentage points.](figures/fig03.svg){fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart. Consultants on tasks AI does well: 12.2% more tasks completed, 25.1% faster. Consultants on a task just beyond AI: 19 percentage points fewer correct answers. Entrepreneurs strong before the study: over 15% better business performance. Entrepreneurs weak before the study: about 10% worse."}

So AI levels execution and widens judgement. A survey of 319 knowledge workers points to the same thing from the inside: the more people trusted the AI, the less critical thinking they reported; the more they trusted themselves, the more they reported [@lee2025critical]. Meanwhile we delegate more. In one large set of conversations with an AI assistant, the share where users handed over a whole task rose from 27% to 39% in under a year [@anthropic2025index].

Handing over a task is not bad in itself. What matters is the loop it starts (Figure 4). In one loop, you ask what matters, the AI explores, you judge, and you come back with a sharper question. In the other, a vague request gets a fluent answer, the answer is accepted, and the next request is no sharper than the last. The first loop is the upper line of Figure 2. The second quietly pulls it down.

![**Figure 4.** Two loops with the same tool. What differs is who asks the question and who judges the answer. Schematic, my own.](figures/fig04.svg){fig-alt="Two circular loops. Supercharged: you ask what matters and why, AI explores options, you judge by testing and doubting, you reframe a sharper question; each turn, you grow. Surrendered: a vague request, AI answers fluently, accepted as is, next request no sharper than the last; each turn, you shrink."}

## 4. Effort builds the skill, and the wish

The second loop costs more than skill. It also costs motivation.

In four experiments with over 3,500 people, working with a generative AI made the work better. But when people then moved to a task on their own, the gain did not carry over, and they reported less intrinsic motivation and more boredom [@wu2025]. Perhaps the tool had done the part of the work that made it interesting.

This fits what psychology has long said about motivation. People are moved from the inside when three needs are met: *autonomy*, the sense of choosing what you do; *competence*, the sense of getting better at something hard; and *relatedness*, doing it with and for others [@ryan2020]. An AI that sets the task and does the hard part can take away the first two without anyone noticing. An AI used to explore questions you chose, on problems you are learning to master, can feed all three.

That is why I worry most about children. An adult who hands a task to AI still has the skill built before. A child who never builds it has nothing to fall back on, and may never discover the pleasure of having worked something out. In a school in Turkey, nearly a thousand high-school students practised mathematics with one of two AI tools (Figure 5). With a plain chat assistant, practice grades rose by 48%. With a tutor designed to give hints instead of answers, they rose by 127%. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. Students who had used the plain assistant scored 17% *lower* than students who never had AI. Students who had used the tutor did about as well as those without AI [@bastani2025]. Similar results appear in essay writing, where students using ChatGPT wrote better essays but learned no more, and reflected less on their own thinking [@fan2025], and among junior developers learning a new library, who scored 17% lower on what they had learned when AI wrote the code for them [@anthropic2026skills].

![**Figure 5.** Practice with AI, then an exam without it. Change in grades compared with students who never had AI [@bastani2025].](figures/fig05.svg){fig-alt="Grouped bar chart. During practice with AI, grades rose 48% with a plain chat assistant and 127% with a tutor that gives hints. In the exam without AI, the plain assistant group scored 17% lower than the control; the tutor group about the same."}

The good news is in the same studies: design matters. A tutor that asks you to try first, and a learner who asks "why?", keep the effort where it belongs. Learning needs friction, and so does joy.

Spinoza gave a definition of joy that fits this exactly: joy is our passage from a lesser to a greater perfection, the feeling of our own power to act increasing [@spinoza1677]. In this sense joy is not having the answer. It is becoming able to find it. A tool that hands us the answer can give us the result and take the joy away. Spinoza ended his *Ethics* with a sentence every student could keep: "all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare."

## 5. Setting the problem: imagination and judgement

If solving becomes cheap, the skills that matter most are those of the middle ring: creativity, imagination and judgement. Imagination is the ability to see a problem nobody has written down yet, and to picture a world that does not exist yet. Judgement is knowing which of those problems deserves months of your life.

Einstein said it plainly. "The formulation of a problem is often more essential than its solution, which may be merely a matter of mathematical or experimental skill," he wrote with Leopold Infeld; raising new questions "requires creative imagination and marks real advance in science" [@einstein1938]. Ten years earlier he had put it more briefly: imagination is more important than knowledge, because knowledge is limited [@viereck1929].

Psychologists later measured it. In the 1970s, they found that art students who spent more time *finding* their problem, exploring and changing it before committing, produced more original work and had more successful careers years later [@getzels1976]. The philosopher Donald Schön wrote that professionals do not simply solve the problems given to them: they *set* them [@schon1983]. What is new is that this is becoming the scarce part. In a large study, research ideas written by a language model were rated *more* novel than ideas from experts [@si2025ideas]. But when 43 researchers spent over 100 hours each carrying the ideas out, the AI ideas lost much more of their score, and their advantage disappeared [@si2025gap]. An idea that sounds new is cheap. Knowing which one is worth pursuing is not.

There is also a trap. When writers used AI-generated ideas, their stories were rated more creative, but the stories became more similar to each other [@doshi2024]. If everyone draws from the same model, the model's defaults become everyone's ideas. The creative edge lies in what you bring that the model would not: your experience, your taste, your stubborn questions. And creativity can be taught. When the OECD measured the creative thinking of 15-year-olds for the first time, scores varied widely between education systems: the OECD average was 33 out of 60, and Singapore reached 41 [@oecd2024pisa].

Under creativity and judgement lies a more basic skill, and I think it is the first one to teach: **epistemic literacy**, the ability to tell information from knowledge. AI gives us unlimited information, fluent and confident. None of it is knowledge until someone has done some work on it (Figure 6). The last step, being able to explain and defend it without the tool, no machine can take for you, because it happens in you. Montaigne asked the same of a child's education more than four centuries ago: better a well-made head than a well-filled one [@montaigne1580]. AI can fill any head at no cost. The making is still ours to do.

![**Figure 6.** From information to knowledge. AI can help with every step, but the last one happens in a person. Schematic, my own.](figures/fig06.svg){fig-alt="Five rising steps. Information: a statement you have read or been given. Sourced: you know where it comes from and how it can fail. Tested: you know what would show it is wrong, and you looked. Connected: it fits, or clashes, with what else you know. Knowledge: you can explain, use and defend it without the tool."}

## 6. What a machine will not care about

Now the outer ring of Figure 1, which I believe matters most.

Aristotle opened his *Metaphysics* with the sentence "all men by nature desire to know" [@aristotle]. Not to possess answers: to know. The desire comes first, and it is ours. A machine works on whatever it is given. It does not care whether the problem matters, whether the answer is beautiful, or whether anyone will ever use it. A result is not valuable in itself. It is valuable to someone: a person with a need, a hope, an idea of how we should live. Deciding what is worth doing is not a technical step; it is a human one.

The philosopher Bernard Suits imagined a utopia where machines do all the work. What would people do there? His answer: play games, which he defined as "the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles" [@suits1978]. We climb mountains although helicopters exist. We still play chess, decades after a computer beat the world champion, and, as we saw, we play it better. The obstacle is unnecessary; the climb is the point. When machines can solve a problem, solving it ourselves becomes a choice, and choices are where meaning lives.

Some questions may stay out of reach forever, for us and for any machine: why there is something rather than nothing, what a good life is, what all of this means. Albert Camus wrote about Sisyphus, condemned to push a rock up a hill forever, and concluded that "one must imagine Sisyphus happy" [@camus1942]. The struggle toward the heights is enough to fill a human heart. I do not read this as resignation. I read it as a description of what makes us human: we keep asking, keep climbing, and find joy in it even without a final answer. Einstein, who knew better than most how far reason can reach, wrote that "the most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious," the source of all true art and science [@einstein1930]. What we cannot reach is not only a limit. It is also what keeps us looking.

A machine may one day reach the top of every hill faster than we can. It will not be glad to be there. That gladness, the motivation to begin, the meaning found on the way, the joy of understanding something for yourself, is not a slower version of what machines do. It is the reason any of it is worth doing.

## 7. Conclusion

The question "what remains for humans?" is usually asked as a race. On speed, the race is over, and that is fine. What remains is the part that was always ours: choosing which problems are worth our time, judging the answers, and caring about them. AI can make us climb higher than ever, as it did for Go players, if we keep making the effort. It can also make the climb feel pointless, if we let it take the part that gave us joy.

So for ourselves: write the question before opening the tool, decide what a good answer looks like, and keep doing some things by hand for the pleasure and the skill. For our children: let them try first, teach them to ask "how do you know?", reward good questions as much as right answers, and leave room for boredom and play, where imagination grows. The machine will find answers. Whether they matter, and the joy of looking for them, is up to us.
